Affinity
ăf-fĭn´ĭ-tĭ
n. (alliance by marriage; kinship contracted rather than born — Hebrew chathan, to make oneself a son-in-law)
Latin affinitas, relation by marriage, from ad and finis, a border — those whose lands, and so whose houses, adjoin. The Hebrew verb means to become a son-in-law by marriage.

Biblical Definition

Affinity in Scripture is alliance made by marriage, and every occurrence is a warning. Solomon's reign opens with it: “Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter, and brought her into the city of David” (1Ki 3:1) — recorded before the dream at Gibeon and the wisdom, and the seed of the wives who turned away his heart in his old age. Jehoshaphat, a good king, made the same mistake with a worse man: “Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab” (2Ch 18:1). The next verse takes him to Ramothgilead in Ahab's chariot, where a prophet asks him why he helps the ungodly, and his son later marries Athaliah, who murders the royal seed. Ezra, in the great confession, states the principle: “Should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations? wouldest not thou be angry with us till thou hadst consumed us, so that there should be no remnant nor escaping?” (Ezr 9:14). Paul's rule is the same in the New Covenant: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness?” (2Co 6:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines affinity as the relation contracted by marriage between a husband and his wife's kindred; distinguished from consanguinity, which is relation by blood.

expand to see more

AFFIN'ITY, n. The relation contracted by marriage, between a husband and his wife's kindred, and between a wife and her husband's kindred; in contradistinction from consanguinity or relation by blood.

2. Agreement; relation; conformity; resemblance; connection.

3. In chemistry, the attraction which takes place between the particles of substances of different kinds.

CONSANGUIN'ITY, n. The relation of persons by blood; kindred by birth.

Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 18:1 — "Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab."

1 Kings 3:1 — "And Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter, and brought her into the city of David, until he had made an end of building his own house, and the house of the LORD, and the wall of Jerusalem round about."

Ezra 9:14 — "Should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations? wouldest not thou be angry with us till thou hadst consumed us, so that there should be no remnant nor escaping?"

2 Corinthians 6:14 — "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?"

Modern Corruption

Alliance with what God has separated from is defended as strategy, influence, or generosity, and the ruin it brings arrives a generation later when no one connects the two.

expand to see more

The narratives are unusually clear about the delay. Solomon's affinity with Egypt is recorded at the beginning of a reign of unmatched glory; the harvest — wives who turned away his heart, high places for Chemosh and Molech, a kingdom torn in two — comes many chapters later. Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab looks like statesmanship; the fruit is his son's marriage to Athaliah and the near extinction of the house of David. Compromise is judged by what it produces at length, and it almost never produces it soon enough for the man who made it to be warned by it.

Paul's rule in 2 Corinthians 6:14 must be handled with the same care Scripture uses. It is not a command to withdraw from unbelievers — Paul says explicitly elsewhere that this would require going out of the world, and Christians are to eat with them, work with them, and be blameless among them. The yoke is the binding partnership: marriage first of all, and any alliance in which a believer's course is set by an unbeliever's aims. Ezra's question is the one to ask of any such union: should we again break thy commandments? The word again is the point — he was speaking to a people who had already been consumed once for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chathan (H2859), to become a son-in-law, make affinity — 1 Kings 3:1, 2 Chronicles 18:1, Ezra 9:14, Deuteronomy 7:3; Greek heterozugeo (G2086), to be unequally yoked.

expand to see more

Hebrew chathan (H2859) — to make oneself a son-in-law, to contract affinity; 1 Kings 3:1, 2 Chronicles 18:1, Ezra 9:14.

Hebrew chathan as a noun — a bridegroom or son-in-law; the same root, which is why marriage is the whole idea.

Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be yoked with one of another kind; 2 Corinthians 6:14, its only occurrence.

Deuteronomy 7:3 gives the original prohibition, and states the reason in verse 4: they will turn away thy son from following me.

Every occurrence of the word in Scripture is followed, sooner or later, by trouble for the house that made it.

Usage

"“Joined affinity with Ahab” — and the fruit came a generation later."

"“Should we again break thy commandments” — Ezra's word is again."

"“Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers”."
